what_its_for: Tepotinib is a cancer medicine used to treat adults with a certain type of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) that has spread to other parts of the body. It works in patients whose cancer has a specific genetic change called METex14 skipping alteration. Your doctor will do a test to confirm you have this genetic change before starting this medicine.
how_to_take: Take tepotinib by mouth once a day with food. Swallow the tablet whole — do not crush, cut, or chew it. Try to take it at the same time every day. If you vomit after taking your dose, do not take another tablet that day — just take your next dose as scheduled.
dosing: The usual adult dose is 450 mg (one tablet) taken by mouth once daily with food. Your doctor may lower your dose or ask you to stop taking it temporarily if you have side effects. Never change your dose on your own without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose and it has been less than 8 hours since your scheduled time, take it as soon as you remember with food. If it has been more than 8 hours, skip the missed dose completely and take your next dose at the regular time the following day. Never take two doses on the same day to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store tepotinib tablets at room temperature between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep the tablets in their original container with the lid tightly closed. Keep away from moisture and heat. Keep this medicine out of reach of children and pets. Do not flush unused medicine down the toilet — ask your pharmacist about the best way to dispose of it.
what_to_avoid: Avoid grapefruit, grapefruit juice, and Seville oranges (often found in marmalades) while taking tepotinib, as they can increase the amount of medicine in your blood and raise your risk of side effects. Tell your doctor or pharmacist about ALL medicines, vitamins, and herbal supplements you take, including over-the-counter drugs, since many medicines can interact with tepotinib. Avoid becoming pregnant while taking this medicine — it can harm an unborn baby. Both men and women should use effective birth control during treatment and for a period after the last dose. Do not breastfeed while taking tepotinib.
when_to_call_doctor: Contact your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: sudden or worsening shortness of breath, cough, or fever (possible lung problems called interstitial lung disease or pneumonitis); swelling of your legs, ankles, or feet (fluid retention); sudden weight gain of more than 5 pounds in a few days; severe nausea, vomiting, stomach pain, yellowing of skin or eyes, or dark urine (possible liver problems); blurry or changes in vision; signs of an allergic reaction such as rash, hives, swelling of face or throat, or difficulty breathing. Also tell your doctor about any unusual or bothersome side effects you notice.
when_it_works: Some patients begin to see a response to tepotinib within the first few weeks to months of treatment, but results vary from person to person. Your doctor will do regular scans and tests to check how well the medicine is working. It is important to keep taking tepotinib every day as prescribed, even if you do not feel sick, unless your doctor tells you to stop.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Do not use tepotinib during pregnancy because it can harm your unborn baby. Use effective birth control during treatment and for at least one week after your last dose if you are a woman who can become pregnant, or if you are a man whose partner can become pregnant. Do not breastfeed during treatment and for at least one week after your last dose. Liver problems: If you have moderate or severe liver disease, your doctor may adjust your dose or monitor you more closely. Kidney problems: Dose adjustments are generally not needed for most patients with kidney disease, but tell your doctor about any kidney conditions you have. Older adults: Tepotinib has been used safely in older patients, but your doctor will monitor you carefully for side effects.
